title: Jordan Sees Bigger Threat From Israel Than Iran
gist: Despite nearly 300 Iranian missiles/drones striking Jordan during the Iran war, a Temple University Jordan expert's on-the-ground conversations find Jordanian officials and commentators far more fearful of Israeli West Bank annexation, which even in its mildest form could push up to 500,000 Palestinian refugees into a kingdom already structurally unable to seal its porous border or absorb the demographic shock.

insights.claim: Nearly 300 Iranian missiles and drones bombarded Jordan during the Iran war, including a July strike that killed three American soldiers and prompted a petition from more than 100 Jordanian activists demanding U.S. forces leave — yet Jordanian officials, journalists, and commentators describe their dread over Israel's accelerating West Bank annexation drive as far greater than their frustration over the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: Contradicts the Western media narrative (that Iranian strikes are the top threat to Jordanian stability); investors and policymakers should weight Israeli-annexation scenarios, not just the Iran war, as the primary near-term Jordan-stability risk.
insights.locator: Yet my recent conversations with Jordanian officials

insights.claim: Under the Oslo Accords' three West Bank zones, Areas A and B (Palestinian Authority-administered) contain most of the West Bank's 3 million Palestinians, while Area C — nearly two-thirds of the territory, home to roughly 250,000 Palestinians and Israel's largest settlement projects — is under full Israeli control.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline territorial/demographic map needed to size any annexation-driven refugee-flow scenario into Jordan.
insights.locator: The Oslo Accords divide the West Bank into three administrative zones.

insights.claim: A Jordanian strategist estimates that even the 'best-case' annexation scenario — Israel absorbing only Area C and East Jerusalem, preserving a rump Palestinian Authority — is anticipated to push up to 500,000 Palestinian refugees into Jordan, while a full annexation of Areas A, B, and C would dissolve the PA entirely and produce a much larger population transfer.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: A concrete, sourced refugee-flow estimate (500,000 minimum) gives a quantifiable basis for modeling humanitarian, fiscal, and political stress on Jordan under any realistic annexation scenario.
insights.locator: even the 'best-case' scenario of annexing Area C

insights.claim: Jordan hosts U.S. forces at a dozen bases as a key logistical hub for U.S. Central Command and is slated to receive more than $2 billion in U.S. economic and security assistance this year — more than any Middle Eastern country except Israel.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: Quantifies Jordan's outsized strategic dependency on, and value to, U.S. Middle East posture — a factor in how much leverage Jordan actually holds over Washington in an annexation crisis (the author argues: less than it appears).
insights.locator: Jordan hosts U.S. forces at a dozen bases

insights.claim: Jordan's economy is already under stress with roughly 83 percent public debt, 24 percent poverty, and 45 percent youth unemployment — a fiscal and social base that would be severely strained by absorbing a large new refugee population.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: These specific fiscal metrics (83% debt, 45% youth unemployment) quantify Jordan's limited absorptive capacity — relevant for sovereign risk assessment on Jordanian debt and any donor/IMF program design.
insights.locator: Absorbing the newcomers would greatly stress a moribund economy

insights.claim: Jordan shares a 60-mile rugged, porous frontier with the West Bank, just 20 miles from Amman (home to nearly half the national population), unlike Egypt, whose flat, securitized 8-mile Gaza border is further insulated by the 130-mile-wide Sinai desert — meaning Jordan's much smaller military cannot realistically seal its border against a refugee influx.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: A specific geographic/military comparison explaining why Jordan, unlike Egypt with Gaza, cannot replicate a hard border-closure strategy against Palestinian displacement — a key differentiator in regional refugee-containment capacity.
insights.locator: Jordan, by contrast, shares a 60-mile rugged frontier

insights.claim: Jordan's uneasy ethnocracy — Transjordanian tribes staffing the state and military, Palestinian Jordanians driving the economy with limited political voice — traces to the 1970 Black September conflict, and for decades the cause of Palestinian statehood functioned as a social 'safety valve' bridging this divide by giving both groups a shared external cause.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific domestic political mechanism (a shared external cause defusing an internal ethnic fault line) that formal Israeli annexation would remove — a mental model for understanding Jordan's internal stability risk beyond simple refugee-capacity math.
insights.locator: Behind Amman's concern is the fraught history

insights.claim: The formal death of Palestinian statehood via annexation would amplify Transjordanian xenophobia while fueling new Palestinian demands for political representation and citizenship — demands that, in an authoritarian system banning major opposition like the Muslim Brotherhood, risk triggering cycles of repression, protest, and volatility.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: Frames a concrete causal chain from annexation to Jordanian domestic instability, useful for scenario-planning Jordan political risk beyond the immediate humanitarian dimension.
insights.locator: Annexation by Israel and the formal demise of Palestinian statehood

themes.theme: Why Israel's calculus toward Jordan has shifted

insights.claim: Israel historically valued Jordan as a stable buffer state protecting its longest land border, but that strategic logic has faded as regional threats have been neutralized: Hamas is 'a shadow of its former self,' Hezbollah has been decapitated, the Assad regime is gone, Iraq is consumed by sectarianism, and Iran remains mired in unwinnable conflict with the U.S. and still lacks nuclear weapons — while the 2020 Abraham Accords normalized ties with four Arab states.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: Explains the structural (not merely ideological) reason Israeli annexation risk has risen: with regional adversaries degraded, Israel no longer needs Jordan as a buffer, removing what had been a key strategic brake on annexation.
insights.locator: First, the strategic need for Jordanian stability

insights.claim: Calls for West Bank annexation have moved from fringe, far-right settler Zionism into the Israeli political mainstream: the Knesset passed a symbolic sovereignty motion, and most parties — including some projected to win October's general elections — now endorse some form of annexation, alongside accelerating settlement construction and land-law changes in Areas B and C.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: Signals annexation is no longer a fringe scenario but plausible mainstream Israeli policy post-October elections — a scenario investors in regional infrastructure, energy, and sovereign debt should now weight as a base case rather than a tail risk.
insights.locator: inside Israeli politics, calls for annexation have radically shifted

themes.theme: Jordan's limited options and reliance on Washington

insights.claim: If West Bank annexation proceeds, Jordan's playbook is to nullify the 1994 peace treaty, sever ties with Israel, close the King Hussein Bridge, militarize its border, and press the U.S. to intervene — but the author argues this response would be undercut because Jordan would need massive U.S. assistance to handle any refugee influx at the very moment it was threatening to revoke U.S. basing rights.
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: Highlights an internal contradiction in Jordan's deterrence posture: its main threat (revoking U.S. base access) is least credible exactly when it most needs U.S. support, weakening Jordan's actual leverage in an annexation crisis.
insights.locator: this would not be enough to mitigate the fallout

insights.claim: Trump currently publicly opposes Israeli annexation of the West Bank, but Jordanians worry Washington will side with Israel if forced to choose, recalling that Trump previously pushed King Abdullah to accept Palestinian refugees from Gaza; a Jordanian journalist remarked, 'Ask the Gazans how hoping for Israeli restraint worked out,' then 'ask the rest of the world how Trump keeping his promises is working out.'
insights.speaker: Sean Yom
insights.so_what: Captures deep Jordanian skepticism that current U.S. opposition to annexation is a durable guarantee — a reason not to assume U.S. policy alone will prevent the scenario this piece is warning about.
insights.quote: Ask the Gazans how hoping for Israeli restraint worked out," then "ask the rest of the world how Trump keeping his promises is working out.
insights.locator: As one Jordanian journalist acerbically told to me
